newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hostile parliament ponders making Yeltsin quit.
newsitem.headline: Hostile parliament ponders making Yeltsin quit.

text.p: A prominent communist lawmaker urged the Russian parliament on Tuesday to force President Boris Yeltsin out of office because of his persistent ill health, but other opposition leaders said the move had no chance of success.
Communist Viktor Ilyukhin said the State Duma's security committee, which he chairs, agreed the initiative after heated debate. "It means Yeltsin will be dismissed," he told reporters.

But the speaker of the State Duma lower house, fellow communist Gennady Seleznyov, conceded the constitutional provisions for ousting an ailing head of state were "very hazy" and forecast that the parliamentary move would lead to nothing.

Asked by reporters what the consequences of the committee's motion would be, he replied: "None." It will, however, be discussed by the Duma's legal department before going to parliamentary party groups in a week or so.

The committee's motion called on the house to declare "the premature cessation of Yeltsin's powers due to his persistent incapacity, through the state of his health, to carry out the duties of president of the Russian Federation".
It said that, as laid down in the constitution, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin should stand in for three months while new presidential elections were organised.
Alexander Kotenkov, Yeltsin's representative in the Duma, said the move had no legislative basis and was simply an attempt to stir up "political scandal".
He said that according to the relevant article of Russia's 1993 constitution, only the president could decide whether his own health was too weak to remain in office.
The article states only that the president "ceases his functions" if his health is too poor to carry out his duties. But it is not clear how that is defined or who defines it.
Yeltsin came down with pneumonia just two weeks after returning to the Kremlin following a heart bypass operation on November 5, and he has been in hospital since last Wednesday.
He has not been fully fit since a recurrence of heart trouble shortly before his re-election on July 3.
Parliament has little power to oust the president.

The communists are the biggest party in the Duma, but it is unlikely they could build the two-thirds majorities in both houses and the swift backing of the Constitutional Court, all of which would be needed to impeach Yeltsin.

The communists threatened impeachment proceedings in November after Yeltsin agreed to Chechen separatist demands to remove all remaining Russian troops from their region. But the move, like an initiative in late summer to introduce compulsory health checks for senior officials, went nowhere.
